title: Train for Power, Not Just Strength
hook: Strength is how much force you can produce; power is how fast you can produce it. A few speed-plus-strength moves build the agility that keeps you nimble and injury-free.
key_points: Power = generating force quickly, which is different from raw strength.
Speed-plus-strength moves train your body to produce force rapidly.
That kind of training improves agility — reacting and changing direction fast.
It also helps prevent injury by preparing the body for sudden, real-world movements.
content_html: Most exercise advice focuses on strength — how much force your muscles can produce. But as NPR's Marielle Segarra reports, there's a companion quality worth training: power, which is how fast you can produce that force.
extra_html:
The distinction is practical. Lifting a heavy box is strength; jumping, sprinting, or catching yourself when you stumble is power, because it demands force now. Movements that combine speed and strength train this rapid force production directly, and the payoff is agility — the ability to react, accelerate, and change direction quickly.

That matters well beyond sports. The same capacity that makes an athlete nimble also helps an ordinary body handle the sudden, unplanned demands of daily life, which is why this kind of training can help prevent injuries. You don't need to add hours to your week; folding a few explosive movements into a routine you already do is enough to start building it. As always, ease in gradually and scale to your own fitness — power work is meant to be quick and controlled, not reckless.

related.title: Why Strength Training Matters
related.hook: Cardio gets the glory, but lifting, resistance bands, and bodyweight moves protect something running can't: the muscle and bone you'll rely on for decades.

related.title: The Strength-Training Sweet Spot for a Longer Life
related.hook: A 30-year study of 147,000 people points to a modest target: about 90–120 minutes of strength training a week was linked to the biggest drop in risk of dying.

related.title: How Much Exercise You Actually Need
related.hook: The headline number is smaller than most people fear: about 150 minutes of moderate activity a week — roughly 20-some minutes a day — moves the needle on your health.

flashcards.prompt: What's the difference between strength and power?

choices.text: Strength is how much force you can produce; power is how fast you produce it
They mean the same thing in exercise
Power only matters for competitive athletes

flashcards.explanation_html: Power combines speed and strength — the ability to generate force quickly — which is what agility and many everyday movements depend on.

flashcards.prompt: Beyond agility, what's a practical benefit of training power with speed-plus-strength moves?
flashcards.back_html: Injury prevention. Training the body to generate force rapidly prepares it for the sudden, real-world movements — catching yourself, changing direction — that cause injuries.
